name: Tanning gummies / supplements

lead: These are chews or pills, often with carotenoids, marketed to make skin look tanner.
No tanning pill is FDA-approved, and no trial supports the gummy format.

paras: Carotenoids such as canthaxanthin deposit in fat under the skin and tint it golden-orange.[2]
High-dose canthaxanthin has been linked to retinal deposits, liver injury and hives;[2] beta-carotene to lung cancer in smokers at high doses.[1]

lead: Tanning gummies and supplements are oral products marketed to boost or deepen a tan, typically containing carotenoids such as beta-carotene. A related older category, tanning pills, used canthaxanthin, a carotenoid that deposits in body fat and gives a golden-orange tint.[1][2]

The US FDA has said no tanning pills are approved and has sent warning letters to sellers, calling such products adulterated cosmetics because they contain an unsafe colour additive.[2] The American Cancer Society states beta-carotene is not FDA-approved for tanning.[1] No clinical trial of a tan-boost chew for appearance has been located.

paras: Canthaxanthin is permitted as a food and feed colour, but not as a tanning agent. In the late 1980s reversible crystal deposits in the retina were reported in some people taking very high doses from tanning pills, and the FDA links such pills to canthaxanthin retinopathy, reported liver injury and hives.[2] A 2011 study reported no lasting structural changes.[2]
High synthetic doses of beta-carotene have been linked to higher lung cancer rates among smokers.[1]

timeline.event: Retinal crystal deposits reported with high-dose canthaxanthin tanning pills.[2]
